source_document.body:
Westinghouse Electric Company is investing approximately $1 billion in a new nuclear fuel factory in Hopkins, South Carolina, with construction underway and production expected to begin in 2030. The building will sit alongside the company’s existing Columbia Fuel Fabrication Facility in Richland County.
What’s Related
The factory will produce low-enriched uranium plus (LEU+) for nuclear power plants. Westinghouse says the fuel can help reactors generate more electricity and run longer between refuelings, reducing the time they must shut down to replace fuel.
The investment will bring commercial-scale production of the fuel to the Columbia site, serving existing reactors and future Westinghouse AP1000 reactors worldwide. The company describes the project as the first new fleet-scale nuclear fuel factory built in the United States in more than 50 years.
South Carolina’s Coordinating Council for Economic Development approved job development credits for the expansion , although the state did not disclose their value.
A different manufacturing process
Westinghouse says the existing plant’s layout and manufacturing technology cannot accommodate the planned commercial production of higher-enrichment fuel. The expansion will place that work in a purpose-built facility next to the current plant.
The building will use more automation and a “dry” manufacturing process similar to one already used at Westinghouse’s factory in the United Kingdom. The company says the process will reduce chemical use and lower the potential for environmental impacts.
The Columbia facility, built in 1968, has more than 1,200 employees. It produces fuel pellets, rods, assemblies, and components for customers around the world and other Westinghouse manufacturing plants.
“A strong American nuclear industry starts with a secure, domestic supply of nuclear fuel,” said Ted Garrish, assistant secretary for nuclear energy.
Construction, suppliers, and hiring
Westinghouse expects several hundred contractors to work on the project at its peak, alongside an internal team of approximately 30 to 50 people. The company says the construction will create opportunities for local contractors, subcontractors and suppliers.
Some of the new manufacturing technology will require additional technical skills. Westinghouse says it is working with local technical schools, colleges, and universities to help prepare employees for that work.
A study commissioned by Westinghouse and conducted with researchers at the University of South Carolina’s Darla Moore School of Business projects $4.9 billion in statewide economic impact over 10 years, including approximately $3.8 billion in Richland County.
The operating benefit Westinghouse is pursuing centers on keeping reactors running longer between fuel changes. Discussing the initial deployment in 2025, Westinghouse Nuclear Fuel President Tarik Choho said: “LEU+ fuel is a perfect example of how we can help reduce the number of outages in nuclear power plants.”

At the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting this weekend, Merck will showcase three late-stage trials of its Kelun-Biotech–partnered TROP2-directed antibody sac-TMT that VP of Chemistry Alan Northrup says gets the payload release “just right.”
Twelve years ago, Merck won FDA approval for the PD-1 inhibitor Keytruda, heralding a new era of cancer treatment—and opening the door to billions of dollars in revenue. Now, with immuno-oncology seemingly on the verge of its next breakthrough , Merck is looking to stake a new claim on the market—this time in the growing space of antibody-drug conjugates.
While the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) market is crowded with candidates, Merck Vice President of Chemistry Alan Northrup believes the company’s Kelun-Biotech–partnered TROP2 ADC is “just right.”
ADCs, which marry the targeting properties of antibodies with the cancer-killing capabilities of cytotoxic drugs such as chemotherapy in hopes of effectively destroying tumor cells while sparing the healthy ones, “remain one of oncology’s most attractive modalities,” Truist Securities said in an Oct. 12 note to investors, “but a crowded pipeline raises the bar for differentiation.”
H.C. Wainwright agreed, writing in a Sept. 28 Deep Dive on the space that “the ADC boom could reshape oncology, defend Merck’s $30B+ [Keytruda] franchise, and reward drugs that overcome resistance or keep patients on therapy.” Sac-TMT, specifically, “could preserve Merck’s central role in frontline oncology beyond Keytruda’s December 2028 primary U.S. patent expiration,” the analysts continued. They added that replacing conventional chemotherapy with ADCs while retaining Keytruda in treatment regimens could address the same large opportunity pursued by PD-(L)1/VEGF bispecific antibodies, which Vision Lifesciences projects will be worth $30 billion by 2032.
Merck’s pipeline currently includes six ADCs, a company representative confirmed, including the B7-H3 directed ifinatamab deruxtecan (I-DXd), the Nectin-4-directed MK-3120 and the Daiichi Sankyo–partnered patritumab deruxtecan. The subject of most attention, however, is Merck and Kelun’s sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT), a TROP-2-targeted ADC in development for a range of indications, including bladder, breast, cervical and endometrial cancer.
The Goldilocks zone
TROP2-directed ADCs are fairly new to the market. The first such drug—Gilead Sciences’ Trodelvy—was greenlit by the FDA in April 2020 for patients with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. Three years later, AstraZeneca and Daiichi Sankyo’s Datroway was approved for the same disease.
Northrup explained that most ADCs—including Trodelvy and Datroway—have a reversible payload linkage to the antibody, while sac-TMT has an irreversible linkage, which keeps the drug stable in the blood until it reaches the tumor.
“You’re trying to find that Goldilocks zone,” he told BioSpace . Some linker payloads are “too hot,” so the payload is released throughout the body, and some are “too cold,” meaning their release is slow once they hit the tumor. “[Sac-TMT] is right in that middle zone where it’s just right.”
This is key to successful treatment, Northrup explained, because when a payload is released early, it is free to circulate through the body, causing myriad issues, including anemia and neutropenia—a condition in which the body has an unusually low number of neutrophils, which attack bacteria and other invaders. Merck believes these adverse effects are due to free payload. On the other hand, if payload release is delayed too long, “you may have also hit a lot of the on-target tissues as well, where TROP2 is expressed in other parts of the body.”
The irreversible linker was part of what drew Merck to Kelun nearly four years ago when the New Jersey giant committed upwards of $9.4 billion biobucks in December 2022 to work with the China-based biotech on seven ADC candidates for cancer targets.
“When we first met with Kelun and started talking with them about their technology, I think we were really impressed by this bifunctional linker because it was really unique in the field,” Northrup said. Merck was watching the development of Datroway and Trodelvy, “and we saw this as something that would be very unique in the field and would get it just right.”
So, is the proof in the proverbial porridge? “I think the trials speak for themselves,” Northrup said.
Sac-TMT will be featured in three late-breaking sessions at the 2026 European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress , which begins Friday in Madrid.
Sac-TMT’s clinical program
One of Merck’s ESMO late-breakers will feature the Phase 3 OptiTROP-Lung06 trial in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In results that read out in July, sac-TMT plus Keytruda meaningfully improved progression-free survival (PFS) vs. the first-line standard of care (immunotherapy plus chemotherapy), meeting the trial’s primary endpoint. The result established another breakthrough, according to Leerink Partners at the time: The first direct proof-of-concept for an ADC that could replace standard of care platinum-based chemo for first-line NSCLC.
Lung cancer
Kelun’s Merck-partnered ADC notches late-stage NSCLC win alongside Keytruda
The Phase 3 results are the first direct proof-of-concept for an ADC replacing platinum-based chemo in a first-line standard-of-care regimen for non-small cell lung cancer, according to Leerink Partners. The readout also represents the second late-stage win for the Merck and Kelun-Biotech asset, called sac-TMT.

2 min read

It was also the first Phase 3 trial of an ADC combined with a checkpoint inhibitor to meet its primary endpoint in first-line driver gene–negative and PD‑L1–negative non-squamous NSCLC, Kelun said in its July 14 press release .
RBC analysts at the time called the trial success “another positive for Merck’s sac-TMT franchise” as it extends the sac-TMT/Keytruda combo from the PD-L1-positive population into the more challenging PD-L1-negative segment.
Meanwhile, in their Oct. 12 note, Truist analysts said that “Sac-TMT and [Datroway] establish key efficacy and safety reference points for next-wave ADCs, with TROP2 remaining the most clinically advanced target.”
In the same slot on Sunday, Kelun and Merck will discuss final overall survival (OS) data from the Phase 3 OptiTROP-Lung04 trial, which pitted sac-TMT against platinum chemotherapy in EGFR-mutated NSCLC after progression on a treatment that blocks the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. The risk of disease progression or death was 51% lower for patients taking the ADC, which met the trial’s primary endpoint, Kelun reported in October 2025. OS was a key secondary endpoint of the trial.
And on Monday, sac-TMT’s successful Phase 3 TroFuse-005 trial in advanced endometrial cancer will be showcased in the Presidential Symposium. In May, the partners reported that TroFuse-005 hit its primary endpoint at an interim analysis, demonstrating significantly better OS and PFS compared to chemo in patients who had undergone prior treatment with platinum-based and anti-PD-1 therapies. The companies promised to provide more details at an upcoming medical congress, which was expected to be ESMO.
It hasn’t all been smooth sailing for Merck’s ADC pipeline, though. The pharma and partner Daiichi Sankyo withdrew an application for accelerated approval of I-DXd in extensive-stage small cell lung cancer after the FDA found that the companies’ data package did not meet the criteria.
“As a field, we can always continue to get better at delivering precisely to the tumor,” Northrup said when asked whether there is a limit to what ADCs can do. He provided two ways in which this can be done: more specific targeting and a more efficacious linker payload, “making sure that you can hold tight to the antibody and release where you want to in the tumor.
“I think Sac-TMT does that very well.”
Cancer
Merck’s billion-dollar Kelun bet pays off as TROP2 improves survival in endometrial cancer
Merck and Kelun-Biotech’s antibody-drug conjugate significantly improved progression-free and overall survival in a pivotal endometrial cancer study, though the companies have yet to specify when they plan to file for approval.

Mercedes-Benz Introduces All-New CLA Shooting Brake to Australia, Pricing Kicks Off at AU$70,800
17 photos
Photo: Mercedes-Benz
The premium German automaker from Stuttgart, Mercedes-Benz , has taken to the Land Down Under the latest iteration of the CLA Shooting Brake with both mild-hybrid gasoline and EV powertrains.
Mercedes-Benz isn’t idle in Australia this fall, and just a few days ago they introduced the all-new Mercedes-Benz C-Class Electric starting at AU$105,700 or about $73,850 at the current exchange rate. Earlier this month, they also brought the first-ever Mercedes-Benz GLE plug-in hybrid models to the region, and that was just the main news for October – and the month isn’t over yet.
Now, the focus is on the latest Mercedes-Benz CLA series, which was recently put through a real-world safety test where the company showed the “world’s first” public high-speed side-impact crash test involving two CLAs: a CLA Shooting Brake with an electrified internal combustion engine was shot into the driver’s side of a fully electric CLA – both vehicles were travelling at 56 kph or about 35 mph.
Back to Australia, the local division of the premium German automaker is bringing the all-new Mercedes-Benz CLA Shooting Brake to the Land Down Under starting from AU$70,800 (MRLP) and AU$72,990 (MRLP), respectively. That’s almost $50k and over $51k at the current exchange rate. And the reason we have two different MRLPs (Manufacturer’s Recommended List Price) is simple: Mercedes is bringing both the CLA 200 with a 48V mild-hybrid powertrain as well as a CLA 200 Shooting Brake Electric with a rear-wheel drive setup.
The new generation of the Mercedes-Benz CLA Shooting Brake arrives in Australia, sharing its design up to the B-pillar with the CLA Coupe version, but featuring a different rear-sloping design, a panoramic glass roof, the optional Sky Control with e-shade, as well as the AMG Line among the standard goodies, with 18-inch AMG five-spoke alloy wheels and additional perks.
The all-electric Shooting Brake will be recognized via the illuminated front panel incorporating 142 chrome-look LED stars “arranged in the signature Mercedes-Benz pattern. Integrated into the distinctive shark-nose front-end design, this illuminated treatment gives the electric model its own visual identity.” Practicality is also the name of the game here: a 455-liter (16 cu. ft.) trunk can be expanded to 1,290 liters (45.55 cu. ft.), and there are also 40:20:40 rear seats.
The interior gets the Mercedes-Benz Operating System (MB.OS) with MBUX navigation, 5G connectivity, wireless smartphone charging and smartphone integration as standard, plus the optional MBUX Superscreen. Under the hood resides a mild hybrid 1.5-liter engine and a 1.3 kWh battery pack, reaching a peak power of 120 kW and 250 Nm (161 hp and 184 lb-ft) of torque.
The electric version has RWD as opposed to FWD on the hybrid, a two-speed transmission, and 165 kW plus 335 Nm (221 hp and 247 lb-ft) of total system power. The 800-volt architecture enables 22-kW (AC) and up to 320-kW DC recharging, while the WLTP range is up to 511 km (318 miles).

The $100,000 H-1B visa fee has significantly affected who biopharma companies hire, according to two experts. It’s not the only program adjustment affecting foreign-born job seekers’ odds of working in the U.S.
Recent and proposed changes to the H-1B visa program are making it less likely that those born outside of the United States will find employment at U.S. biopharmas.
One of the most recent and significant adjustments to H-1B visas is the $100,000 fee for new petitions, which a high cost for employers, especially smaller companies. Intended to prioritize American workers by restricting entry into the U.S. by nonimmigrants seeking jobs in specialty occupations, the fee went into effect last year. Last month, the Trump administration extended it through Sept. 21, 2027.
Court challenges have resulted in two federal judges blocking the fee. The first ruling was in June, two months after U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) began accepting H-1B cap-subject petitions for applicants whose registrations had been selected. The second came late last month, after the fee extension.
Despite the rulings, the $100,000 fee has affected who biopharmas employ. Dave Bowers, managing director and global head of life sciences search firm EPM Scientific, told BioSpace , “The fee effectively shut the door on hiring talent from overseas.”
U.S. biotech hiring teams, he said, have pivoted to focus on talent already in the United States, such as those transferring their H-1B visa from one employer to another, U.S. nationals, U.S. graduates, U.S. citizens and green card holders.
“Whereas before, we would look at international communities and candidates based outside of the U.S., there is a laser focus on those that are authorized to work in the U.S. today,” Bowers said.
There has been a particular hiring challenge, he noted, for roles in computational biology, AI in drug discovery, cell and gene therapy, process development and biostatistics.
“These are often talent pools that have been international in their makeup, and clients are now limited in who they can look to identify to drive their program or their project forward,” Bowers said.
Audrea Golding, a partner at immigration law firm Fragomen, has also seen the $100,000 fee impact biopharma hiring. She told BioSpace that when the H-1B lottery opened earlier this year, the not-yet-blocked fee was a significant consideration for biotech and pharma companies, especially startups.
“A lot of companies did not put people into the lottery, believing that the $100,000 fee was going to be payable if that person was outside of the U.S. or had to go outside of the U.S. before their H-1B could be granted,” Golding said.
The lottery, or selection process, takes place when H-1B visa registrations are so high that subsequent petitions would surpass the annual cap of 65,000. An additional 20,000 petitions for those who have earned a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. institution are exempt from the cap.
Recent data underscores companies’ reluctance to participate in the H-1B visa program this year. In May, USCIS announced that the number of properly submitted H-1B registrations dropped from 343,981 in fiscal year 2026 to 211,600 in fiscal year 2027, a 38.5% decrease.
Still, Golding expects that next year, some companies will err on the side of using the H-1B lottery given the recent rulings blocking the fee.
“I think that was a big lesson from this year was that the companies who made the decision not to put people into the lottery because of the concern of the $100,000 fee ultimately lost the ability to bring people in that they otherwise could have had for their companies because of the legal injunction,” she said.
Who the $100,000 fee impacts most
Both Bowers and Golding agreed the H-1B fee’s impact on hiring is most felt by smaller companies such as startups and small to medium-sized biotechs, for whom $100,000 is a prohibitive amount.
I think the reality is Big Pharma can absorb a large cost for a critical hire, whereas a series A company can’t necessarily do that.
Dave Bowers, EPM Scientific
“I think the reality is Big Pharma can absorb a large cost for a critical hire, whereas a series A company can’t necessarily do that,” Bowers said.
He also noted that the H-1B visa policy further narrows the pool of early phase research and development (R&D) talent. For employers, Bowers said, that means a longer time to hire and, at times, paying premium salaries for niche and individual skills. From a job seeker’s perspective, he noted that companies’ hesitancy to hire R&D professionals who need H-1B visas has some candidates choosing to stay in academia in their own countries.
Golding highlighted the $100,000 fee’s impact on those who came to the United States as students, completed their four-year program and were looking forward to starting their careers in the U.S. There has been uncertainty about whether employers that recruit them will sponsor them, she explained.
“To have that concern around whether or not a company is going to ultimately then be willing to put them into the lottery was pretty nerve wracking, I would say, for a lot of folks,” Golding said.
Additional H-1B hurdles
Another recent change to the H-1B visa program that Golding said affects biopharma hiring is the new weighted selection process, which favors allocating visas to higher-skilled, higher-paid people. Starting in fiscal year 2027, which runs from Oct. 1, 2026, to Sept. 30, 2027, those at the lowest of four wage levels get one entry into the selection pool, while those in the highest level receive four.
That allocation could soon change. In March, the Department of Labor (DOL) proposed adjusting how it calculates wage levels for various visa programs, including the H-1B, so levels better align with what is paid to similarly employed U.S. workers. Such revisions could reduce the incentive for employers to use visa programs to replace, rather than supplement, U.S. workers by employing lower-paid foreign-born professionals, according to DOL.
The proposed changes, Golding said, could result in someone falling from a higher wage level to a lower one and receiving fewer entries into the selection pool. She noted that students have been concerned about how that would affect their chances to get selected in a lottery.
Two other proposed H-1B visa changes that Golding said could affect biopharma hiring were put forth by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in August:
A $103,265 fee for all H-1B cap-subject petitions. The fee is meant to generate revenue to recover some of the federal government’s costs for administering the immigration system.
Revised eligibility for H-1B cap exemptions. The goals for that proposal include providing greater scrutiny for employers that have violated program requirements. DHS has not specified what the revisions would entail.
Regarding the revised eligibility proposal, Golding noted that biopharma research organizations that are now cap exempt could lose that status.
Looking ahead to 2027, Bowers expects that biopharma companies’ reluctance to hire and employ people who require H-1B visas will stay high, especially for early career roles. However, he added, demand isn’t going anywhere.
“The U.S. needs more skilled workers within biomanufacturing, quality, R&D, etc., not less,” he said. “Those that win are going to develop U.S. talent and are going to be in a position to fill those specialist roles quickly.”

Tesla has begun volume production of its electric Class 8 Semi truck at its Nevada factory , a major milestone as the company prepares to expand commercial deliveries in the U.S. and enter the European market in 2027.
The Austin, Texas-based electric vehicle manufacturer confirmed the production milestone Wednesday in its third-quarter earnings report, listing installed annual manufacturing capacity of 25,000 Semis at its Nevada facility.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk also highlighted the development during the company’s earnings call with analysts on Wednesday.
“We also began production of the Tesla semi-truck in Q3, our Class 8 heavy-duty truck,” Musk said during his opening remarks.
Tesla (Nasdaq: TSLA ) provided updated performance figures for the Semi in its third-quarter earnings presentation, highlighting the truck’s range and energy efficiency and its high-volume production line at the company’s Nevada factory.
“The top variant can go 500 miles at a full 82,000 lbs gross combination weight while achieving an efficiency of 1.7 kWh/mile,” Musk said. “That efficiency allows the Tesla Semi to use a third of the energy used by a comparable diesel truck to haul the same payload. In a transportation market where energy is one of the largest components of total cost per mile, this will provide a meaningful advantage to Tesla Semi operators.”
However, Tesla did not disclose how many Semi trucks were produced or delivered during the quarter, and its reported manufacturing capacity does not necessarily reflect its current production rate.
Tesla reported third-quarter revenue of $28.05 billion, essentially unchanged from $28.1 billion during the same period last year.
Tesla reported adjusted earnings of 48 cents per share in the third quarter, down 4% from 50 cents per share a year earlier. GAAP earnings fell 44% to 22 cents per share.
GAAP net income attributable to common stockholders fell 43% year over year to $787 million, compared with $1.37 billion in the third quarter of 2025.
Operating income declined 56% to $718 million, while operating expenses increased 39% to $4.78 billion.
Tesla reported $1.53 billion in free cash flow and ended the quarter with approximately $45.45 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments.
The company produced 464,391 passenger vehicles during the quarter and delivered 486,532, down approximately 2% from the same period in 2025.
Tesla also revised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to approximately $20 billion as it continues investing in manufacturing, artificial intelligence, robotics and energy infrastructure.
Metric | Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | Change
Adjusted (non-GAAP) diluted EPS | $0.48 | $0.50 | -4%
GAAP diluted EPS | $0.22 | $0.39 | -44%
Tesla’s expansion plans extend beyond North America, with the company targeting its first European customer deliveries of the Semi by the end of 2027.
During the IAA Transportation conference in Hannover, Germany, in September, Dan Priestley, head of Tesla’s Semi program, said the company planned to begin European customer demonstrations during the first half of 2027.
The initial European trucks will be manufactured at Tesla’s Nevada factory.
“What we’re working on right now is lining up customers that are highly interested in experiencing the truck through demonstrations in the first half of next year, with the opportunity then to take delivery, targeting by the end of next year,” Priestley said during the conference, according to FreightWaves’ earlier reporting .
Tesla has also outlined plans to begin deploying more than 100 Megacharger stalls in Europe in 2027, with a charging capacity of up to 1.2 megawatts per stall.
Priestley previously said the company had not made a decision on establishing a European Semi manufacturing plant, citing available capacity at its Nevada facility.
Tesla’s third-quarter earnings presentation did not provide a new European delivery schedule or disclose the number of trucks allocated to the market.
Tesla’s manufacturing milestone follows its selection as the lead supplier for a 2,500-truck battery-electric Class 8 order announced in September.
The order is being coordinated through ZET SCALE, the Zero-Emission Truck Shipper-Carrier Alliance Leading Electrification, organized by Catalyst Mobility and Smart Freight Centre.

CarPlay Is Getting the Google Maps Feature Many Android Auto Users Hate
15 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
The time has come for Apple users to discover the actual power of Gemini. And this might not happen in a good way. It’s no secret that Gemini has malfunctioned in the most frustrating ways on Android Auto, and now the new AI-powered assistant is bringing its magic to CarPlay.
Google has announced that Gemini is now live in Google Maps on CarPlay . Users in the United States are getting it first, while the rollout in the rest of the world is still underway.
I’ve already received Gemini in Google Maps on CarPlay with an iPhone 15 Pro here in Europe, and the feature works exactly as you’d expect it to work. You just ask Gemini for directions, places, or anything else that exists in Google Maps, and you get a detailed answer.
Gemini is supposed to be an upgraded version of Google Assistant, though many people have described it as way too chatty , especially behind the wheel. This is an environment where users are supposed to be focused entirely on the road and avoid any distractions, so a digital assistant that keeps rambling on in the middle of the drive isn’t necessarily helpful.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution However, Google promises that Gemini will provide valuable information in a conversational way. Indeed, I’ve already interacted with Gemini, and the way you talk feels significantly more natural. You can keep the conversation going and submit follow-up requests based on what you’ve just said.
For example, you can ask Gemini for “a coffee place that serves the best cappuccino in this neighborhood,” and the AI-powered assistant will use its superpowers to look for nearby locations, check their ratings on Google, dig deep into reviews, and use any available data to determine the shop that serves that perfect cappuccino.
After showing the results, you can continue the conversation with something like “is it expensive?”, and Gemini will continue the search, knowing that you’re talking about the cappuccino. It’ll once again search for additional data and let you know about the dollars you’ll have to pay if you stop at this coffee place.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Eventually, you can have Gemini set up a certain location as your destination in Google Maps, so you can begin navigation to this location.
In my time with Gemini, I really didn’t notice anything wrong or buggy, and to be honest, I was impressed with how responsive it was. It certainly feels like a welcome upgrade, and at some level, Gemini on CarPlay feels a lot more refined than Gemini on Android Auto.
This wouldn’t be a shocking thing, considering Google has previously shown impressive love for Apple’s platform, but Gemini on Android Auto has been extremely buggy since it started rolling out in late 2025.
That is why many Android Auto users who received the new AI power used the option to go back to Google Assistant when it was still available. Many people downgraded to Google Assistant, hoping Google would refine Gemini before it was enforced for everybody.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution This eventually happened last month, when Google Assistant was completely retired, and Gemini became the only option for Android Auto users. Many people described it as Cortana - Microsoft’s digital assistant, once supposed to be a Google Assistant and Siri competitor, that ended up becoming a flop - revealing that Gemini couldn’t even call 911 or make phone calls.
Gemini also allows users to submit traffic reports, and the best thing about this feature is that you don’t have to remember certain phrases to do it. Gemini can understand what you say and figure out what type of report it has to submit.
For example, you can say that “wow, traffic has become a nightmare on this small street,” and Gemini knows that you mean there’s bumper-to-bumper traffic on that road. It can then submit a heavy traffic report to the app.
Traffic reports have become an essential part of the experience with Google Maps, primarily after Google brought this feature to Android Auto and CarPlay in 2024. The feature was originally launched on mobile devices in 2019, but Google never looked interested in expanding it beyond smartphones.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Many people believed this was a way to avoid the cannibalization of Waze, another Google-owned navigation app whose main selling point is the crowdsourced traffic report engine.
Google eventually changed its mind in 2024, bringing the ability to pin hazards to the map to CarPlay in early 2024 and to Android Auto later in the same year. Google is now encouraging users to contribute traffic data, also importing police reports from Waze to make the information provided to users in Google Maps more accurate.
Compared to Waze, Google Maps is focused only on the most common traffic reports, such as accidents, roadworks, and speed radars. Waze supports a significantly wider range of reports, including objects on the road, broken traffic lights, flooded roads, and potholes, and this is considered to be the only big reason why Google Maps and Waze continue to exist as separate applications.

MISUMI Americas has launched a foundation with $2 million in seed funding to help students pursue careers in engineering, manufacturing , and supply chain. The MISUMI Imprint Foundation will fund scholarships, hands-on learning programs, and partnerships between schools and manufacturers across the United States.
What’s Related
The foundation is MISUMI Group's first corporate giving organization in its 63-year history. Its first grant cycle is expected to open in early 2027, and the company plans to expand the foundation internationally over time.
MISUMI is also inviting its global suppliers to contribute through a Partner Network. Participating suppliers will make voluntary annual contributions and join an advisory board that meets twice a year to set grant priorities and jointly announce awards.
The foundation will direct grants toward three areas:
Scholarships and access: Need-based aid for first-generation and underrepresented students attending vocational schools, trade programs, and universities .
Hands-on learning: Equipment for manufacturing labs, engineering team sponsorships, maker spaces, and student hackathons.
School and industry partnerships: Coursework based on manufacturing problems, internships, apprenticeships, mentoring, and career guidance .
RELATED STORIES: MISUMI Launches Americas Business to Bring Parts Under One Roof | MISUMI Americas CEO Dave Evans Discusses the Importance of Building Fast With AI
Helping students start manufacturing careers
MISUMI, which supplies mechanical components and assemblies, says the foundation responds to hiring difficulties it sees among both customers and manufacturing partners. Unfilled machinist, programmer, and technician jobs can limit how much work a manufacturer can accept, according to the company.
The foundation’s focus extends beyond engineers to the people who build, maintain, and inspect equipment. MISUMI cited demand for CNC programmers, toolmakers, quality and maintenance technicians, automation specialists, and production supervisors.
“MISUMI has spent decades supplying the components engineers design into machines, so we know exactly who builds the physical world,” said Dave Evans, president and CEO of MISUMI Americas.
Evans said the approach draws on designer Buckminster Fuller’s concept of a trim tab, a small secondary rudder that helps turn a large ship.
“You don’t change a system by moving all of it at once. You find the small lever in the right place and you keep pushing. A scholarship that lets one student finish a degree is a small thing. Thousands of them, over a decade, are not.”
Bringing suppliers into the grant program
The supplier program offers three participation levels: Founding Partner, Growth Partner, and Community Partner. MISUMI did not disclose the contribution amounts for each tier or how much individual grants will provide.
The arrangement gives suppliers a way to contribute through an existing foundation without creating their own giving organizations. Schools, other organizations, and suppliers can find information about grants and participation through MISUMI’s Imprint platform.
“For more than sixty years, MISUMI has supported the people who make things,” said Arata Shimizu, CEO of MISUMI Group. “The Imprint Foundation is the first time we have built an organization dedicated to the next generation of builders.”

Securing financing that allowed an exit from academia, leaving ecology and evolutionary biology for biomedical engineering and shifting from business development to entrepreneurship are among key turning points for three biopharma professionals.
The BioSpace 40 Under 40 cohort have a host of impressive accomplishments that have garnered attention among their peers and within the biopharma industry. To see what shaped their success, BioSpace asked three honorees to share the turning points in their careers.
Lex Johnson: making the leap from academia to industry
Lex Johnson, Dispatch Bio
For Lex Johnson, chief platform officer of Dispatch Bio, the turning point was securing financing for the company he helped start while doing postdoctoral work at the University of Pennsylvania. Johnson recalled taking many Zoom calls with investors during a tough time for the biotech market following the COVID-19 pandemic. Most of that outreach did not lead to investment.
“You have 100 of these conversations, and 90 of them go nowhere, and then of the 10 that go somewhere, eight of those die on the vine two calls later,” Johnson told BioSpace . “And so, you get into this mode where ‘Yeah, this would be nice if it happened, but who knows if it’s even really real?’”
Johnson’s efforts paid off. He secured financing from the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy (PICI), the first of two founding investors, and Dispatch Bio went on to launch in 2025 with $216 million in series A funding. That funding was critical not only for the company’s work to create a universal treatment for solid tumors but also for Johnson’s transition out of academia into industry.
“That meant going from being just someone with an idea to being someone who was responsible for making sure that we had a lease in place, making sure that we bought all the equipment that we needed, making sure that we hired the right people and that those people were structured in ways that were efficient so that we got the work done in the ways that we did,” he said. “And so, that was a huge change in the way that I had to do my work as well.”
Making such a transition can be challenging for young founders, Johnson noted.
“You have to see yourself as that source of authority if you want to be an effective leader, at least in my mind,” he said. “And you need to see yourself as a decision maker when decisions need to be made. Some of those decisions are really small, some of those decisions are really big, but at the end of the day, somebody needs to say, ‘This is the direction we’re going,’ and so I think that was also a big area of growth personally.”
Johnson described his journey out of academia to his current role leading teams focused on innovative targeting strategies, T cell signaling pathways and therapeutic delivery as amazing.
“It’s been incredible to be able to lead something that started as a kitchen table project, and then it morphed into five, 10 people in a lab, and now we’re 60, 70 people, and we’ve got a drug in the clinic,” he said. “I’d do it all over again.”
Amy Kauffman: switching fields, walking in patients’ shoes
Amy Kauffman, Bristol Myers Squibb
Amy Kauffman, senior principal scientist in sterile product development at Bristol Myers Squibb, pointed to two turning points in her career. The first, she told BioSpace , was leaving ecology and evolutionary biology for biomedical engineering.
“I really loved how nature worked, and over time, I realized that I wanted to actually do more,” Kauffman said. “I really wanted to understand how problems work, how to solve them—and do things that’s going to make a bigger impact instead of just being the next Jack Hanna or David Attenborough.”
Kauffman moved into biomedical engineering in graduate school, which proved challenging. She noted that she had to play a lot of catch-up to be on the same level as her peers. She also had to work with mentors who weren’t always supportive of her move into engineering. That experience, Kauffman said, made her supportive of others who want to transition into fields such as chemical or mechanical engineering.
“I want to see more people like that because they bring a different perspective of what they know in their past, and they see things very differently than some of us who are so close to the lens that we miss small details,” she said.
Kauffman’s second turning point was learning she had celiac disease during her postdoctoral training.
“So, really, it was getting a closer look at what it’s like from a patient’s perspective when we’re developing things like delivery systems and what it’s actually like to sit in that chair, receive an infusion or even when you go in to get a standard vaccine, how much work does it take to go through it?” she said.
Kauffman, whose work at BMS focuses on long-acting injectables, said her personal experience with celiac—and other autoimmune conditions—made her appreciate even more that every step taken on the bench impacts a patient’s experience.
“Being able to kind of put that together, it really just kind of pushed me back into the drug delivery world of ‘OK, how do we do this better? How do we make sure that these scary diseases that require a lot of treatment are as easy as possible for people?’” she said.
Reflecting on whether one turning point stands out more than the other, Kauffman said they’re equally weighted.
“If it wasn’t for changing into my field, I don’t think I would be doing the type of research or discoveries that I’m doing now,” she said. “But I also don’t think those discoveries would be nearly as passionately explored if it hadn’t been through kind of the lens as a patient too.”
Christine Zhang: moving from finance to biotech, then entrepreneurship
Christine Zhang, BridgeBio
Like Kauffman, Christine Zhang also identified two turning points. The executive director and Evanesco program lead at BridgeBio told BioSpace the first came at the start of her career. Initially, she worked as a healthcare private equity investor at TPG and as a biotech investment banker at Goldman Sachs. It was a great training ground, she said, “But one thing that I learned after a couple years working in finance is that I really missed the science. So, that was when I decided to make a big pivot and change industries.”
Zhang took a role at biotech BridgeBio, where she initially worked on corporate strategy for the lead asset now known as Attruby. The drug, which received FDA approval in 2024, treats transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), a potentially fatal heart disease.
After seeing Attruby make its way from clinical trials to commercial launch, Zhang had her second career turning point: moving from business development to entrepreneurship. Seeing an unmet need for depleter therapies that could go beyond halting ATTR-CM and instead reverse it, she created the BridgeBio affiliate Evanesco.
“It really started off as a passion project, but the more I dug into the idea, the more I really believed that this could be a great opportunity,” Zhang said. “And, it would cement Bridge Bio’s dedication to the ATTR-CM space and to this patient community, because even though we had one commercial therapy, we don’t just rest on our laurels. We continue to innovate.”
Zhang’s months of preparation for presenting Evanesco to BridgeBio’s CEO and board of directors included partnering with a network of experts. That network included biopharma professionals working in antibody engineering and discovery; ATTR-CM cardiologists; and BridgeBio and industry leaders. Zhang would ask her network to identify potential program obstacles, then go home and determine how to mitigate the concerns before presenting proposed solutions. If those solutions did not address the concerns, she would return for another conversation, telling her network, “We will just go through this process until either you convince me that Evanesco is not a good idea, in which case we shouldn’t fund it, or I convince you that this is a good idea, I properly mitigate all of your concerns, and then I would love to get your backing to support this program.”
Zhang got that backing, which allowed her to hire a team of scientists, build a lab in Palo Alto, California, and start discovery experiments. A development candidate nomination that will be BridgeBio’s first antibody program is expected to move into the clinic between 2027 to 2028.

source_document.body:
What changes when robots join the warehouse team? Manish Kapoor , Founder and CEO of Growth Catalyst Group , shares lessons from Archway’s Minnesota fulfillment center, including how employees’ jobs have changed and how to decide which tasks are worth automating .
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: What led Archway to add robots at its Maple Grove fulfillment center?
Manish Kapoor: We didn’t start by saying, ‘we need robots.’ We started with the problem we were trying to solve. This was a joint initiative with Blackhawk Network, a fulfillment client of ours, that specializes in global branded payments with gift cards, eGifts, rewards and other payment products. Together, we looked at what the Maple Grove operation needed to deliver as demand grows. We focused on productivity, accuracy, speed, space and scalability.
Customers expect orders quickly, they expect them to be right, and they need flexibility as demand changes. We needed an operation that could respond to changing demand while making better use of our people and the space we already have.
RELATED STORIES: Six Trends Changing How Mobile Robots Work in Warehouses | Robots for the Rest of Us: Warehouse Automation Gets Easier
That led us to Quicktron’s goods-to-person solution. It combines high-density storage with tote-handling robots, tote transport robots and intelligent picking workstations. Instead of employees spending time walking through the warehouse to find inventory, the robots retrieve the right totes from storage and move them to the picking stations where our people fulfill the orders . It allows us to store more products in a relatively small footprint while moving thousands of product units through the system every hour. For me, that’s the important point. We didn’t choose automation because we wanted robots in the building. We defined what the operation needed to achieve, then found the technology that could help us achieve it.
SC247: Can you walk us through how the robots and employees work together to fill a gift card order?
“Customers expect orders quickly, they expect them to be right, and they need flexibility as demand changes”
Kapoor: It’s a goods-to-person system, so rather than having an employee walk through the warehouse to find and move inventory, the system brings the inventory to them.
Within the automation area, we have tote-handling robots working in a high-density storage system, tote transport robots and picking workstations. The robots retrieve and move the appropriate totes through the system and bring them to the workstation where our people can complete the picking process.
That takes a lot of unnecessary movement out of the job. Our employees can focus on fulfilling the order while the robots handle much of the movement of inventory around them.
That’s the relationship we want between people and automation. Use the technology for the work it is good at, and give our people better tools to do their jobs and the time back to focus on human-centric tasks
SC247: You report a 300% increase in productivity. What did you measure, and what was the comparison?
Kapoor: The improvement is more than 300% in productivity within the automation area, compared with the previous process. Before implementing the technology, we established a baseline so we could understand whether it was solving the problems we had identified. Productivity was obviously a major measure, but we were also looking at accuracy, speed and how effectively we could use the available space. The system can now process thousands of product units every hour, and we’ve reduced time to market by 50%. That means we can get products where they need to go much faster while making the fulfillment operation more responsive. That’s the important part of measuring automation.
SC247: How have employees’ day-to-day jobs changed since the robots arrived?
Kapoor: The biggest change is that the product comes to the person, rather than the person spending so much time going to the product. In a traditional warehouse process, there can be a lot of walking and movement involved in finding inventory and getting it where it needs to go. The goods-to-person system takes a lot of that movement out of the process.
Our people remain a critical part of the operation. What we’re doing is giving them technology that helps them work more efficiently and allows us to process more volume with the workforce we have. That’s how I think about automation. It’s not robots versus people. It’s about how you bring the two together to build a better process.
SC247: What was the hardest part of getting the robots up and running?
Kapoor: With any automation project, the robot is only one part of the picture. The operating process, software , data and people must work together.
We had an advantage because we have our own warehouse management platform, so we had full control of the software side which helped make the software integration smooth. But, you still need to think through how technology fits into the whole operation, how your people are going to work with it and how you measure whether it is doing what you expected.
I often say transformation takes a village. Archway, Blackhawk Network and Quicktron all brought different expertise to this project. Getting those pieces working together is what turns a technology project into an operational improvement.
“With any automation project, the robot is only one part of the picture. The operating process, software, data and people must work together.”
SC247: Why did you choose these robots, and where do you see humanoid robots fitting into warehouse work?
Kapoor: We started with the problem, not the technology. We knew what we wanted to improve in the operation, and we established the criteria before selecting a solution. We looked at productivity, quality, speed, how effectively we could use the space, and whether the system could scale with the customer. Quicktron’s robotic solution fit those requirements.
The ability to use the vertical space was particularly important for this operation. The robots can move up, down and across, and the goods-to-person model reduces the amount of movement our people have to do. It gave us a solution that worked for the operation we were trying to build.
Humanoid technology is still maturing and not a fit for the problems we solve. As our use cases will continue to grow and change, we’ll continue to stay close to the evolution of this technology.
SC247: How do you decide whether automating a warehouse task is worth the cost?
Kapoor: Before I automate something, I want to understand why we are doing it that way in the first place. If there is waste in the process and you automate it, you are just automating the waste. Then you’ve put technology around it and made that waste harder to remove.
Once you understand and improve the process, you can establish your baseline and decide what technology needs to change. Then you can look at the investment and decide whether the technology is creating value.
Maple Grove is a good example. We established what we wanted to achieve before we implemented the automation and measured the results against that baseline. Productivity more than doubled, quality reached almost 100%, and speed was roughly three times what it had been. For me, that’s how you determine whether automation is worth the investment, if it’s actually solving the problem you started with and have results to prove it.
SC247: What advice would you give a warehouse operator considering robots for the first time?
Kapoor: Don’t start with the robot. Start with the problem and walk your process first. Understand where the waste is and take out what you can before you automate it. Then establish your baseline, because if you don’t know where you started, you won’t know what the technology has improved. You also have to look beyond the individual task. You could make one part of a warehouse significantly faster, but if the next part of the operation can’t handle the additional volume, you’ve just moved the bottleneck. The end goal is to create a better operation for your customer and your people. If automation helps you do that and the numbers make sense, then you have a strong case for it.
Manish Kapoor is Founder and CEO of Growth Catalyst Group .
